Boise Semi in the USA supplies the other 30 %, by air via Chicago. --NOTES: Before we look at Soony in detail: what can go wrong in a supply chain in general? Six things, and none of them is exotic. One: a shipment is late, split into several deliveries, or stuck at a port. Two: a supplier delivers the wrong thing, the wrong version, or too little. Three: the system says a part is in stock, but it is not on the shelf. Four: a contract or a price changes, and nobody reads the small print. Five: something needs a decision, and nobody knows who is allowed to approve the fix. Six: the world happens. Strikes, export bans, weather. This happens every week in every company that buys things. content.text:
The sources mostly back our direction. The biggest gaps are: no Plan B, no count of copies at risk on the cards, no detection of data that stops updating, and no price or cost-per-copy for the business case. Sources: the deep-dive slides (32 slides including speaker notes), both PDFs and both transcripts, all read in full. I wrote nothing to the repo; only scripts and text extracts are in `/Users/jonasstenglein/.claude/jobs/3021cc1a/tmp/research/`.

## 1. What the jury wants to see or will ask

- **Show what we found** (slide 28 notes): "On Sunday we want to see your agents work on Soony's real, messy data, and we want to hear **what they found that Soony's team missed**." Felix's side also said: "some big problems in the data you should already at least try to find… before the data shows."
- **The one rule** (slide 28 notes): "agents that read, decide, act and talk to people. A dashboard on top of a spreadsheet is not enough."
- **Drops are found, not announced** (slide 30 notes): "Your agents have to notice it, work out what it means, and decide whether it matters for Sunday… One example shows something new appearing, the other shows something that stops changing. **Your agents need to watch for both.**"
- **Mistakes** (Judging p.3, "Strong"): "The team can explain **what happens when the system gets something wrong**." Have an answer ready for the 2 minutes of questions.
- **Taste** (Judging p.3): "Soony's team has ten minutes and forty dashboards… **a clear recommendation and one click to act**… the moment a human has to decide."
- **Demo format** (Judging p.4): 3 minutes in the order problem, system ("Live"), business. Tips: "Start the demo early. Slides are support, not the show." "Go deep, not wide." "If the Wi-Fi dies, your demo video saves you. Still, the live run is what counts."
- **Business** (Judging p.2): "Why would Soony pay for it, and **roughly how much**?" Strong means "a number the customer cares about, and a clear path to the next ten customers." Weak means "The market is huge."
- **Autonomy and trust** (Felix, 554s): "in the demo it makes sense that you can like stop at some point and say like here's an approval… **But this can also run autonomously. It should be able to run autonomously.**"
- **Scope** (Felix, 1093s): the product "should be generalizable… don't focus so much on the software actually being able to scale."
- **Handling messy data** (Nils, 848s): "it's not about how deep you know the data but like that **you can handle like this sort of data**."

## 2. Interview quotes for the pitch

**Felix, Senior Buyer**
- On finding out too late (37s): "your tool… has to tell me, **before the supplier does, that something will not arrive. Otherwise I would not use it.**" (Already in our notes.)
- On acting on signals (60s): "not with hundred percent accuracy. But… that you at least try to take action if you see some signals."
- **New**, on why waiting for approvers fails (612s). This supports our phone call when critical: "if we need to wait for approvals of certain people all the time for this critical game release, **it will take ages because they don't look into the notifications, they don't do shit**."
- **New**, on trust building up over time (554s). This is the routines story in his own words: "once they use it and see… that this decision that the AI recommends are mostly or like very often the correct one… **at some point they flip the switch and let it run autonomously.**"
- **New**, on who approves (320s, 377s): "person A has an approval budget of 10,000 euro… [another] four million… a hierarchy." Also: "different for every enterprise… **this is what we actually do, building up those approval chains.**" This lines up with "money always stays human" and with approval limits you can configure.
- **New**, on contradictions (505s): "sometimes one source of information is wrong, sometimes the other. **In the end I don't care. I want that the process works.**"
- On transparency alone (114s): "it solves the problem of transparency, but in the end if it doesn't arrive…"

**Nils, IT**
- **New**, on repetition (230s to 300s), our strongest argument for routines. Asked for his most annoying task: "going into my email box… we got this new receipt coming in… and then me having to put that into our ERP." Asked "For every single order?": "Yeah." Asked whether mails reach him from outside or are forwarded inside the company: "Mostly internal."
- On errors found late (329s): an error gets noticed "weeks or months later"; he then goes "into our table, look, compare… fix it."
- On trust in automation (438s): "I can trust the system. I think there would be less error. **If [it's] uncertain, I would want to know, or if it's a big delivery.**" This fits confidence thresholds on routines.
- On the dream (519s, 740s): "if the SAP is like the ultimate source of truth that would be the best thing… **If I can fully trust my data, I would sleep a lot better.**"
- On wrong receipts (84s): "we reclaim it and then… finance… will handle it." Agents must not edit supplier documents.
- **New**, on the cause (541s): "unclear processes… different people have different preferred ways."
- On scope (191s, 706s): email-only "would already help"; a two-way SAP integration "out of scope for the weekend."

## 3. Numbers for the business case

All of these are from slides 19 to 22 and the brief:
- 487,000 pre-orders. Day-one demand is 640,000 Standard and 72,000 Collector's, every Collector's copy numbered and pre-ordered.
- Still to pack: 128,000 Standard and 25,200 Collector's.
- 30 packing hours left. Collector's needs 28 of them, so it has **2 hours of slack**, and "**every hour it waits for a part costs 900 copies**."
- Standard runs on 3 lines and needs 21 hours, so it has 9 hours of slack.
- Sea from Busan takes 36 days, so "Anything ordered from Asia today arrives after the launch."
- For scale: Lio serves 175+ enterprises, and the six risk types "happen every week in every company that buys things" (slide 26).
- Approval limits from Felix: €10,000 and €4M (his example, not real data).

**Missing:** no source gives a price or margin per copy, or the cost of a missing copy. Maren Vogt (CPO) is the persona for "what a missing copy costs" and we have not interviewed her. If a Sun 09:00 slot is still possible, ask her. Otherwise, state an assumption clearly as one.

## 4. Gaps and contradictions

- **Plan B.** Felix: transparency alone does not ship games. Our cards point out conflicts but do not suggest an alternative. Karton Nowak is the only supplier that can still deliver in time.
- **Impact on Sunday.** Cards should say "X Collector's copies at risk, cell idle Y hours" rather than only "doc ≠ SAP." That is the number the customer cares about.
- **Something that stops changing.** Slide 30 asks us to catch data that goes quiet (`updated_at` frozen). Our document-reading flow does not obviously cover this.
- **"What did you find that they missed."** We need two or three concrete findings ready to name.
- **When the system is wrong.** We need an explicit answer: anchors show where a number came from, routines have limits and can be reverted, money stays with a human.
- **Pricing and the next ten customers.** No price and no named other customer segments yet.
- **Possible tensions with our direction:**
  - Felix "I don't care" which source is right: cards must end in an action, not in a debate over which source wins.
  - Nils: never correct supplier documents. Reclaim instead, and finance handles it.
  - Felix "I would not focus on" detailed approval chains: keep it to one configurable limit.
  - Mail replies do not change portal data, so supplier replies only update our local state.

## 5. Opening wording (first 30 seconds)

- **Option A:** "Soony's head of procurement told us: 'We find out at the dock.' On Saturday Felix, their senior buyer, told us: 'Your tool has to tell me before the supplier does that something won't arrive. Otherwise I won't use it.' The Collector's cell has two hours of slack, and every hour it waits for a part costs 900 numbered copies. So we built agents that read every supplier document, in Korean, Chinese, Polish and English, and catch the problem before it hits the dock."
- **Option B (leads into routines):** "Nils from Soony's IT spends his days copying supplier receipts into SAP, 'for every single order'. Errors surface 'weeks or months later'. Felix told us his approvers 'don't look into the notifications'. So our agents check every document against SAP, call the right person when it's critical, and after one human yes they write a routine for next time. Money always stays human."
- **Closing line:** "As Nils put it: 'If I can fully trust my data, I would sleep a lot better.'"
